name: SD card (9-pin)
description: The full-size SD card's 9 edge contacts. The card supports two bus protocols on the same pins: the native SD/SDIO bus (1- or 4-bit, fast) and a slower SPI mode that most microcontrollers use. Signal names differ between the two modes -- this entry lists both. SD I/O is 3.3 V; there is no 5 V here.

contacts.name: CD/DAT3
contacts.description: SD: card-detect / data line 3 (4-bit mode). SPI: chip select (active low)

contacts.name: CMD
contacts.description: SD: command line. SPI: DI = MOSI (data in to card)

contacts.name: VDD
contacts.description: supply, 2.7-3.6 V (nominally 3.3 V) -- NOT 5 V tolerant

contacts.name: DAT0
contacts.description: SD: data line 0. SPI: DO = MISO (data out of card)

contacts.name: DAT1
contacts.description: SD: data line 1 (4-bit) / SDIO interrupt. SPI: unused (NC)

contacts.name: DAT2
contacts.description: SD: data line 2 (4-bit mode). SPI: unused (NC)

variants: microSD has 8 contacts (drops one ground) but the same signals and both bus modes; a passive microSD-to-SD adapter is just wiring, no electronics.
SPI mode uses only pins 1,2,5,7 (nCS/MOSI/SCLK/MISO) + power/ground; the SD 4-bit mode adds DAT1/DAT2 (pins 8,9) for 4x throughput.
gotchas: SD is 3.3 V. Driving the pins from 5 V logic (a classic Arduino Uno mistake) can damage the card -- level-shift, or use a board with the shifter built in.
Almost every MCU talks to SD cards in SPI mode (pins 1,2,5,7). It's slow compared to native 4-bit SDIO, but simple. Cheap 'SD modules' are just a socket + a 3.3 V regulator + level shifters.
Pin 1 doubles as DAT3 in 4-bit SD mode and as chip-select in SPI mode -- so a 4-bit host and an SPI host use the same pin for very different things.
Cards need a valid init sequence (send CMD0 with CS low to enter SPI mode); just clocking data at a fresh card without the handshake gets you nothing.
notes: Full-size SD 9-pin, SDIO + SPI mode names, cross-checked against Wikipedia's SD pinout table. 3.3V I/O; microSD is the same signals on 8 contacts.
